clue.text: Do your best, without lines, to produce such transport

indicators.note: to do something up is to work on it and rearrange it, so the following words are reworked
without in its old sense of outside, so one piece sits round the other

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged
L is the abbreviation for line, doubled for the plural

explanation.surface: Someone is urged to try hard to bring about a kind of public transport.
explanation.walkthrough: The jumbled letters of 'your best' are written round LL. 'Such' points back to the wordplay: a trolleybus runs on overhead lines, and here the lines are literally inside.
explanation.definitionFit: A trolleybus is an electric bus drawing power from overhead cables, the kind of vehicle the clue describes.

clue.text: A horse drinking nothing alcoholic wants nothing but an alcoholic drink

blocks.note: taken as written
a mare is a female horse
TT, teetotal, means taking no alcohol
O looks like a zero

explanation.surface: A teetotal horse refuses everything but turns out to want a liqueur after all.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface puts 'alcoholic' in twice to confuse; the first is part of the TT piece, the second belongs to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Amaretto is an Italian almond-flavoured liqueur, a sweet spirit served after dinner.

clue.text: I'm spent in a round, but if you're offering...?

indicators.note: to send things round is to turn them about, so these letters get stirred into a new order

blocks.note: the ten letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A drinker complains their money has gone on buying a round, yet still accepts another.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Round' reads as a round of drinks, which fits the pub scene, but it is the signal to jumble 'I'm spent in a'.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is what a pub-goer says when a friend asks what they would like, accepting a glass of beer.

clue.text: Donkey losing head - it swirls

indicators.note: losing its head means the word drops its first letter

blocks.note: neddy is a British pet name for a donkey

explanation.surface: A beheaded donkey is pictured spinning round.
explanation.definitionFit: An eddy is a small whirlpool of water or air turning in a circle against the main current.

clue.text: Trollop held up by Freud's complex will be disappointed

indicators.note: in a down entry, holding a word up turns it to read from bottom to top
something complex is tangled, so the letters of Freud's are muddled
held by means gripped inside, so one piece is surrounded

blocks.note: tart is slang for a loose woman
the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A psychoanalytic diagnosis: a promiscuous woman with a Freudian complex will end up thwarted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Complex' looks like a noun as in Oedipus complex; here it is an adjective signalling the jumble.
explanation.definitionFit: To be frustrated is to be thwarted and let down, the feeling of having hopes go unmet.

clue.text: Ornamentation made with a four-by-two

indicators.note: something made from raw material is formed anew, so these letters are fashioned into a new order

blocks.note: the word four taken two times

explanation.surface: Some decoration is produced using a four-by-two, a piece of timber four inches by two.
explanation.walkthrough: A four-by-two is a length of wood, so the clue looks like carpentry; read literally it is 'four' times two, jumbled.
explanation.definitionFit: Frou-frou means fussy decorative frills on dress or furnishings, showy embellishment.

clue.text: Where Bennett's Englishman was with an American girl

blocks.note: an and a are the same indefinite article
broad is American slang for a woman

explanation.surface: A quiz question about Alan Bennett's Englishman, apparently accompanied by a girl from the US.
explanation.walkthrough: Alan Bennett wrote the play An Englishman Abroad, about the spy Guy Burgess in Moscow.
explanation.definitionFit: The title of the Bennett play places its Englishman overseas, in a foreign country.

clue.text: See 3
A memory's about, but it's over

indicators.note: about here means around, so one piece goes round the other

blocks.note: taken as written
a reminder is a memory prompt; the 's is 'is'

explanation.surface: Someone recalls a memory that is drifting about, yet it is all in the past.
explanation.walkthrough: The memory word wraps round A: REM-A-INDER.
explanation.definitionFit: Over in the sense of left over: the remainder is what is surplus once the rest is taken.

clue.text: Teacher's pet that's fast-breeding must be docked

indicators.note: docking a tail cuts off the end, so the last letter goes

blocks.note: rabbits are famous for breeding quickly

explanation.surface: A teacher's prolific classroom pet needs its tail cut.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Teacher's pet' reads as a phrase for a favourite pupil, but 'Teacher' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A rabbi is a Jewish religious leader and scholar whose title literally means master or teacher.

clue.text: Prisoner captures king at sea, we hear (in the main)

indicators.note: to capture is to hold inside, so one piece goes within the other
what we hear is spoken, so the result is judged on its sound

blocks.note: lag is British slang for a convict
R for rex, Latin for king
alee is the nautical word for on the sheltered side, away from the wind

explanation.surface: A convict seizes a monarch on the ocean, according to rumour.
explanation.walkthrough: LA(R)G followed by ALEE, said quickly, comes out as the answer. The parenthesis marks the definition as an aside.
explanation.definitionFit: In the main is an idiom for mostly or for the most part, the same sense as the answer.

clue.text: Bar offers beer to entertain hospital and university

indicators.note: a host entertains guests within, so one piece is held inside

blocks.note: stout is a dark beer
H is the abbreviation for hospital
U is the abbreviation for university

explanation.surface: A pub provides beer for hosting medics and students.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bar' looks like a pub, which fits the beer, but it is the verb meaning to exclude.
explanation.definitionFit: To shut out someone is to bar them, keeping them from entering a place.

clue.text: Small part, though wide, perhaps?

blocks.note: first meaning: a walk-on role in a film
second meaning: in cricket a wide is a ball out of the batsman's reach, giving a bonus run

explanation.surface: A bit part, though a broad one, seemingly.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket, runs not scored off the bat, such as a wide, are called extras; the question mark marks the wide as an example.
explanation.definitionFit: A film extra plays a background role, and a cricket extra is a run conceded such as a wide.

clue.text: A case of something a farmer might fill to the brim

blocks.note: a farm cart is loaded with produce
a ridge is a raised edge or top, like a brim

explanation.surface: A farmer filling something up as full as it will go.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A case of' suggests an example; here 'A case' is the definition and the rest is the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A cartridge is a casing holding a bullet and its charge, or ink for a printer.

clue.text: Rocky peak avoided amongst inclines with narrow transport

indicators.note: in a down entry the peak is the top letter, and avoiding it means it is left off
amongst means placed in the middle of, so one piece sits inside

blocks.note: a cant is a slope or tilt
Rocky Balboa is the boxer in the Rocky films

explanation.surface: A route through tilted ground skirts a craggy summit, by way of slim vehicles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rocky' wants to be an adjective for the peak, or an anagram signal; it is the boxer, whose surname loses its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: British canals carry narrowboats, long slim vessels, so canal boats are a narrow kind of transport.

clue.text: Hearing piece for organ and brass

blocks.note: the ear is a body organ
the trumpet is a brass instrument

explanation.surface: A musical piece listened to, scored for organ and brass band.
explanation.walkthrough: Organ and brass suggest musical instruments, and 'hearing piece' a concert work; the organ is a body part.
explanation.definitionFit: An ear trumpet is an old horn-shaped device held to the ear to help the deaf hear.

clue.text: Melodramatic production sounds dull, given mistake from Spooner?

indicators.note: the Reverend Spooner swapped the opening sounds of words, so the starts are exchanged

blocks.note: a thud is a dull sound, given means plus, and a blunder is a mistake; swap the opening sounds

explanation.surface: A theatrical show that sounds tedious and botched, as the famously muddled Reverend Spooner might put it.
explanation.definitionFit: Blood-and-thunder describes sensational, violent melodrama, the stuff of lurid stage shows and pulp stories.

clue.text: Pat swallows horribly limp kneidel

indicators.note: to swallow is to take in, so one piece ends up inside
horribly means in a mangled way, so the following letters are scrambled

blocks.note: a cow pat is a lump of dung
the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone called Pat struggles to get down a soggy Jewish dumpling.
explanation.walkthrough: Pat looks like a person's name; it is a cow pat.
explanation.definitionFit: A kneidel is a matzo ball, a small Jewish dumpling served in chicken soup.

clue.text: Parliament, having secured vote, passed round joint

indicators.note: something passed round moves from hand to hand, so its letters end up shuffled
securing something means holding it fast within, so one piece goes inside

blocks.note: the Dail is the lower house of the Irish parliament
the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A parliament wins a vote and a joint is handed about, a scandal in the chamber.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Joint' looks like a cannabis cigarette passed round; it is a woodworking joint.
explanation.definitionFit: A dovetail is an interlocking carpentry joint with fan-shaped tenons fitting matching sockets.

clue.text: Get away! Shed's confused!

blocks.note: scram is a command to clear off
to shed blood is to bleed, so shed stands for bled

explanation.surface: Someone shouts in disbelief that Shed, a fellow Guardian setter, is muddled.
explanation.walkthrough: Shed is the pseudonym of another Guardian compiler, so the surface is a dig at a colleague.
explanation.definitionFit: Scrambled means jumbled or muddled, as in a scrambled message or scrambled thoughts.

clue.text: The problem with pepper

blocks.note: first meaning: a puzzle or conundrum
second meaning: to ... with bullets is to pepper with shot

explanation.walkthrough: 'The problem with pepper' sounds like a complaint about a seasoning; to pepper and to riddle both mean to pierce with many holes.
explanation.definitionFit: A riddle is a puzzling question, and the verb means to pierce something all over with holes.

clue.text: Compiler sold last year for a tenner ...

definitions.text: sold last year for a tenner

blocks.note: first meaning: a Guardian crossword setter's pseudonym

blocks.clueFragment: sold last year for a tenner
blocks.note: second meaning: the British car maker BMW sold for ten pounds in 2000

explanation.surface: A crossword setter apparently sold off cheaply, for a ten-pound note.
explanation.walkthrough: In 2000 BMW sold the Rover car company to the Phoenix consortium for a nominal ten pounds; a tenner is a ten-pound note.
explanation.definitionFit: Rover was both a pseudonym used by a Guardian setter and the name of the British carmaker.

clue.text: Coe's nose, perhaps

blocks.note: surface reading: the nose of Sebastian Coe, the British Olympic middle-distance champion
setter's reading: things that run, as Coe did on the track and as a nose does with a cold

explanation.walkthrough: Sebastian Coe is a British athlete who won Olympic gold at 1500 metres; 'perhaps' marks both him and a streaming nose as examples.
explanation.definitionFit: Coe was an athlete on the track, and a nose that drips with a cold is likewise something that runs.

clue.text: ...  whose beastly pal collects profit, it's said, for another

indicators.note: to collect is to gather in, so one piece is held inside
said means spoken, so a word that merely sounds like profit is wanted

blocks.note: the previous clue's answer is a classic dog's name, and its canine pal has another
Eli was a priest and prophet in the Old Testament

explanation.surface: Continuing from the previous clue: the setter's animal friend gathers a profit on behalf of a colleague.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis links to Rover, read as a dog's name; another stock dog's name is his pal. Fidelio was also a Guardian setter's pseudonym.
explanation.definitionFit: Another refers back to the compiler in the previous clue: this answer was the pen name of a different Guardian setter.

clue.text: Kingdom instrumental to the Scots?

definitions.note: adjective standing for the noun, a musical instrument

blocks.note: first meaning: the Scottish region known as the Kingdom of
second meaning: a small high-pitched flute

explanation.surface: A realm that has been vital to Scotland.
explanation.walkthrough: Fife, a region of east Scotland, is traditionally called the Kingdom of Fife; the fife is a flute played in marching bands.
explanation.definitionFit: The Scottish county has the historic title Kingdom, and the fife is a little military flute.

clue.text: Lunatic can and must find holy refuge

indicators.note: a lunatic thing is crazy and out of order, so the following letters are jumbled

blocks.note: the first set of letters to be rearranged
the second set of letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A madman is able and obliged to seek sanctuary in a church.
explanation.definitionFit: A sanctum is a sacred inner place, a shrine or private retreat where one is safe.

clue.text: Place in which to wash pot

blocks.note: first meaning: a kitchen basin
second meaning: in snooker, to pot a ball is to send it into a pocket

explanation.walkthrough: 'Pot' looks like a pan to be washed up, which fits the kitchen; it is the verb from snooker.
explanation.definitionFit: A sink is a basin for washing up, and to sink a ball or putt means to pot it.

clue.text: Criminal, then virtually all right? On the contrary

indicators.note: virtually means almost, so the word stops a letter short
doing things contrariwise means the opposite way round, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: each word swapped for its opposite: the opposite of all is no and of right is left

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a criminal is more or less fine, then answers no.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On the contrary' does double work: it turns all right into its opposite, no left, and then runs that, missing its last letter, backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A felon is someone convicted of a serious crime, a criminal.

clue.text: Entering branch, seeing red and orange

indicators.note: entering means going into, so one piece sits inside the other

blocks.note: a tine is a prong or branch of an antler
seeing red means being angry

explanation.surface: Going into a branch office, someone is furious and colourful.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Red and orange' look like a pair of colours; red belongs to the idiom seeing red, and orange is the fruit.
explanation.definitionFit: A tangerine is a small, loose-skinned citrus fruit, a type of orange.
